title: Homogeneous ODE
body:
A linear ODE with **zero on the right hand side**:

$$
a_n y^{(n)} + \dots + a_1 y' + a_0 y = 0
$$

"Homogeneous" here means the forcing term is absent, so the equation describes a system left to
itself. With constant coefficients it is completely solvable, and the method is algebra rather than
calculus.

> **Careful, the word is overloaded.** For a *first order* equation "homogeneous" sometimes means
> $y' = F(y/x)$, a different property entirely. In this course, in the linear setting, it means the
> right side is zero. [[Non-Homogeneous ODE]] is the case where it is not.

## The characteristic equation

Guess $y = e^{rt}$. Every derivative brings down a factor of $r$, so the whole equation becomes
$e^{rt}$ times a polynomial, and $e^{rt}$ is never zero:

$$
ay'' + by' + cy = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad ar^2 + br + c = 0
$$

The roots of that polynomial decide everything.

| Roots | General solution | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Real, distinct $r_1 \neq r_2$ | $c_1e^{r_1t} + c_2e^{r_2t}$ | exponential growth or decay |
| Real, repeated $r$ | $c_1e^{rt} + c_2te^{rt}$ | the extra $t$ is needed, see below |
| Complex $\alpha \pm \beta i$ | $e^{\alpha t}(c_1\cos\beta t + c_2\sin\beta t)$ | oscillation, damped if $\alpha < 0$ |

The repeated-root row is the one to remember, because the obvious answer gives only one solution
and a second-order equation needs two. Multiplying by $t$ is the standard repair, and the same
trick reappears in [[Undetermined Coefficients]] for the same reason: the guess collided with
something already present.

The complex row comes straight from Euler's formula, $e^{(\alpha+i\beta)t} = e^{\alpha t}(\cos\beta t + i\sin\beta t)$.
**Oscillation in a physical system is complex roots of its characteristic polynomial**, which is
why a mass on a spring and an RLC circuit are the same equation. See [[Complex Numbers]].

## Why "general solution" means what it does

The solutions of a linear homogeneous ODE form a [[Vector Space]]: add two, scale one, still a
solution. An $n$th order equation gives an $n$-dimensional solution space, so $n$
[[Linear Dependence|linearly independent]] solutions span the lot and

$$
y = c_1y_1 + \dots + c_ny_n
$$

is a general solution because it is a general **linear combination**, not because someone collected
enough cases. Independence is checked with the Wronskian, which is a [[Determinant]]. Initial
conditions pin the $c_i$ down, one condition per constant.

## Related

- [[Non-Homogeneous ODE]]: same left side, a forcing term on the right, and this note's answer is
  half of that one's
- [[Undetermined Coefficients]]: the method for finding the other half
- [[Cauchy-Euler]]: variable coefficients that still reduce to a characteristic equation
- [[Systems of Differential Equations]]: the same idea with a matrix, where the characteristic
  polynomial is literally [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors|the eigenvalue equation]]
- [[Vector Space]] and [[Linear Dependence]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]
- [[Differential Equations]], [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]
